The workshop, bringing together 40 graduates, post graduates and young space researchers from across Europe, contained expert lectures covering subjects like the Moon/Mars environment, systems engineering, architectural design, human factors etc. and culminated in a design exercise which lead to the development of design concepts of Lunar, Martian and Phobos habitat. 

This paper gives an explanation and discussion of the habitats and scenarios developed in the workshop that integrate new technologies, materials and strategies underlining the features of sustainable concepts through detailed discussion and illustrations. 

The added value of this Habitat Design Workshop is the combination of analysis and design of habitat concepts from a systems engineering and natural sciences perspective with an architectural design and human factors perspective.   Reflecting the multi-disciplinarity needed for the development of extraterrestrial human habitats, the participants comprised of students from disciplines such as engineering, medicine, physics, architecture and industrial design.

The MoonMars Working Group believe that overcoming the challenges of a sustainable programme of exploration, utilisation and settlement of the solar system, an interdisciplinary approach to extraterrestrial habitats is essential for success.  The Habitat Design Workshop is an on-going activity and we welcome constructive criticism and suggestions.

Title: Customer Expectations versus Vehicle Performance
Publication: IAC 2005 congress proceedings, 56th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–21 October 2005, Fuduoka, Japan
Abstract:
This analysis investigates in coherences between the two disciplines of customer expectations and launch vehicle performance. For a successful space tourism flight venture it is necessary to under-stand passenger behavior and wishes on the one side and technical feasibility of space transportation systems on the other side. In most cases, a satisfaction of a customer wish is penalized by a lower vehicle performance and vice versa. For example, a launch near Equator increases payload capacity in forms of passenger seats but is less attractive for tourists due to the long journey from their home country to Equator. 

The study is based on test subjects who participated in STMS II. Space Tourism Market Simulation II (STMS II) is an interactive simulation covering various disciplines such as rocket engineering, economics, design, laws, ethics, art, etc. around space tourism to understand and practice coherences about this topic. Participants can choose one out of eight specific groups such as passenger, manufacturer, organization, space travel agency, investor, government, opposition or own created group. They can either cooperate or compete with other groups. The idea of STMS II is to improve participant’s knowledge and skills of space tourism in the fields of strategic decision-making, engineering, teamwork, marketing and entrepreneurial activities.

Keio University’s Rocket Plane Concept is used as reference launch vehicle for STMS II simulation. The importance of the flight verification for innovative concepts or advanced technologies has been repeatedly emphasized, but spaceplane or rocket plane concepts are rarely demonstrated. The concept proposed here is a Horizontal Take-off/Landing (HT/HL) space plane powered by existing rocket engines and winged drop-tanks. For more qualitative investigation, proof-of-concept models (to be called POC model) were designed, manufactured and tested in the wind tunnel to obtain aerodynamic data.  In addition, one of the POC models has flying capability with an engine and a controller to be used for demonstration of the separation process from high-speed.

KEYWORDS: Customer Behavior, Multidisciplinary Aspects, Reusable Launch Vehicle, Performance, Program Planning

Title: Space Technologies and Informatization of Russia
Publication: IAC 2005 congress proceedings, 56th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–21 October 2005, Fuduoka, Japan

Title: ABOUT PART OF SPACE EXPERIMENT IN SOLVING PROBLEM TO PROTECT THE EARTH AGAINST COLLISION WITH ASTEROID
Publication: IAC 2003 congress proceedings, 54th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  29 September–3 October 2003, Bremen, Germany
Abstract:
The obvious illustration of the danger of collision with asteroid is the fact that the whole of Earth surface is strewed with craters from the past collisions. The craters from collisions with the space objects are seen on the Mars and Moon surfaces. The globality of problem to protect the Earth against collision with asteroid witnesses the expedience to draw the efforts of scientists and designers of many countries with the advanced science and technology for its solution.
In spite of the fact that the collision of the Earth with asteroid is the event, which occurs about one time per 100-300 years, it may take place also in the near future. Not only the objects recorded by the Center of small planets, but also unknown ones offer the danger. The reports on the anti-asteroid problem, periodically presented at the IAF congresses, in combination with the reports at the international conferences are the important step on way to create the effective protection of the Earth. A number of submitted conceptions on creation of system for protecting against asteroids, including the conception of authors on creation of the ecologically clean space rocket anti-asteroid systems, need the experimental verification of the theoretical conclusions.
In the report proposed for discussion there are the schemes to perfonn the experiments on influence of the tentative structures of the research modules on the asteroid. The report also deals with the versions to inject the research modules into trajectories, which are the encountering ones in relation to asteroid, for experiments at the collision velocity of about 100 km/s.
In doing so, the following aspects of the planned experiment are elucidated:
- choice of asteroid according to the criterion of combination of the power capabilities of the space rocket system and good conditions for observation with using the ground and space means at moment of collision; - preliminary analysis of trajectories to deliver the module to the asteroid.

Title: COVERAGE OPTIMIZATION OF ELLIPTICAL SATELLITE CONSTELLATIONS WITH AN EXTENDED SATELLITE TRIPLET METHOD
Publication: IAC 2003 congress proceedings, 54th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  29 September–3 October 2003, Bremen, Germany
Abstract: The design of a satellite constellation is often driven by coverage objectives. Many methods have been developed to evaluate the coverage efficiency of a constellation pattern, but they are often restricted to continuous global coverage analyses of satellites on circular orbits. Unfortunately, a global coverage of the planet is not always the most cost effective paradigm. In many cases, it is better to optimize a constellation according to zonal coverage objectives rather than a global one. Moreover, to further improve the zonal coverage of the satellites, we should switch to elliptical orbits to allow the satellites to stay for a longer time in view of the zonal targets around their apogee. In this paper, we will show that with some modifications we can still use Walker’s coverage analysis algorithm based on satellite triplets to assess the coverage efficiency of satellite constellation patterns on elliptical orbits. As an illustration of the method, we will present the most suited symmetrical patterns to cover the Northern hemisphere. These patterns are an extension of the classical Walker constellations. To limit the search domain, but also because of their remarkable stability, we will use only elliptical orbits with a frozen perigee.

Authors: ['A. Caramagno', 'D. Benavente', 'J.C. Bastante', 'V. Fernández', 'Luis F. Peñín', 'J. Rodríguez-Canabal']
Title: G&C DESIGN PROCESS FOR FUTURE FORMATION FLYING AND AUTOMATED
Publication: IAC 2003 congress proceedings, 54th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  29 September–3 October 2003, Bremen, Germany
Abstract:
Several European space missions, whose launch and operational life is envisaged for the next decades, base the achievement of their mission objectives on successful design, coordination and control of the relative motion of a set of SC, ranging from two, as in the case of an Automated Mars Rendezvous (ARV), for instance; to a higher number for Satellite Formations, i.e. up to eight for the Darwin mission. These two classes of mission, apparently very different and heterogeneous in terms of objectives (science or technology demonstration) and operational requirements (level of autonomy), share several commonalities from the Guidance and Control point of view.
This paper focuses on the G&C subsystem, looking at the relevant schemes and architectures, G&C design and analysis methodology, guidance and control algorithms for Formation Flying and Rendezvous Operations. After presenting a generic methodology for G&C design process, and for illustration purposes, a particular application is made to the case of an Automated Rendezvous in a Martian environment, of special significance for the future Space Exploration missions envisaged in the Aurora plan.

Title: TESTBED FOR THE COLUMBUS TERMINAL EXPERIMENTAL COMMS FACILITY
Publication: IAC 2003 congress proceedings, 54th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  29 September–3 October 2003, Bremen, Germany
Abstract: The paper presents ongoing activities to prepare COLUMBUS for communications and multimedia technology experiments, and to design a COLUMBUS Ka/S band terminal to support data transmission. For this purpose, EADS ST, Bremen, has studied several options how to best combine the given system architecture with flexible and state-of-the-art interface avionics and software. These activities have been conducted in coordination with, and partially under contract of, the European Space Agency (ESA/ESTEC). In parallel EADS ST has realized a testbed for multimedia software and hardware testing, which has been co - funded by the Senate of Bremen within the framework of the BEOS R&D programme preparing the establishment of an ISS Operations & Utilization Center. This paper updates and continues IAC-02-T.4.07, presenting the results obtained in late 2002 up to summer 2003.

Title: THE SIMULATION TOOL OF WIDEBAND MULTIMEDIA MOBILE SATELLITE COMMUNICATIONS SYSTEM
Publication: IAC 2003 congress proceedings, 54th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  29 September–3 October 2003, Bremen, Germany
Abstract: The developing trend of modem communications system leans to personality, multimedia and be moveable. In despite of needs of wider band, flexibility access, convenience and rapid services, the development and operation cost of such system must be not very expensive so that it can be accepted by market. There are many uncertain features for such system considered technologies development in the future, and it makes high risks in developing such system. The satellite communications technology lias developed for many years, there are some technical options which can be selected and combined for a certain system. When these options and user requirements, conunercial features and other uncertain features are considered comprehensively, it becomes very complexity and difficult to make a final decision. In tliis paper, a digital simulation tool is presented, which is adapted to investigate the satellite conununications system, specially adapted to study wideband multimedia mobile communications satellite system developed in future. This simulation tool is a set of software packages developed based on commercial software, and lias a hierarchy. The actual using of tliis simulation tool proved that is an effective way in conception design period.

Title: COLUMBUS as engineering testbed for communications and multimedia experiments
Publication: IAC 2002 congress proceedings, 53rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–19 October 2002, Houston, United States
Abstract: The paper presents ongoing activities to prepare COLUMBUS for communications and multimedia technology experiments. For this purpose, Astrium SI, Bremen, has studied several options how to best combine the given system architecture with flexible and state-of-the-art interface avionics and software. These activities have been conducted in coordination with, and partially under contract of, DLR and ESA/ESTEC: Astrium SI shall design and partially implement all provisions for installing a Ka band COLUMBUS Terminal, an advanced digital video system, and high speed data handling avionics. Moreover, Astrium SI has realized three testbeds for multimedia software and hardware testing under own funding.

Title: Engineering tools and validation test beds for new telecommunication satellite multimedia systems
Publication: IAC 2002 congress proceedings, 53rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–19 October 2002, Houston, United States
Abstract:
Satellite telecommunication and broadcasting systems have to adapt to the major evolutions introduced by the emergence of new multimedia services distributed by terrestrial networks. This major adaptation of satellite telecommunication systems implies the use of new technologies and standards, on-board satellites and within the telecommunication ground segment The deeper interaction between space and ground infrastructures induced by these evolutions also leads to additional system complexity.
The definition, design and end-to-end validation of these satellite networks require dedicated engineering tools and validation test beds running the major elements of the telecommunication mission, e.g. on-board and ground equipment implementing the various protocols and algorithms used in the system.
Through two programmes called respectively “Atelier Télécom du Futur” and “Multimedia System Validation Test Beds”,
CNES has been developing since early 2000 an advanced simulation tool and complementary test beds to support engineering activities and cover most of the end-to-end validation needs of these new satellite telecommunication multimedia systems.
This communication aims to present the technical objectives, the logic which has led to propose several complementary means, their main characteristics and development status.

Title: Media-augmented exercise machine
Publication: IAC 2002 congress proceedings, 53rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–19 October 2002, Houston, United States
Abstract:
This paper reviews preliminary work on a project to augment exercise equipment with social, recreational, training or collaborative activities and thereby enhancing the exercise activity and reducing time pressures on the crew. In addition, the machine functions as an interface to a wide range of digital environments allowing for spatial variety in an otherwise confined environment. We hypothesize that the adoption of media augmented exercise machines will have a positive effect on psycho-social well-being on long duration missions. By organizing and supplementing existing equipment, exercise machines, data acquisition hardware, computers and displays, into an interacting system this proposal increases functionality with limited additional mass. A gravity- based testbed augmented exercise machine uses a specialty built cycle trainer as both input to a virtual environment and as an output device from it using sound, visual displays, vibration transducers and variable resistance. The resulting interactivity increases a sense of engagement in the exercise, and provides a rich experience of the digital environments.
The Media Augmented eXercise Machine* (MAXM) project grew out of a series of design studios at the University of Arkansas School of Architecture. Students in a professional architecture program worked on problems related to the inhabitation of Extreme Environments. One design studio, offered during the Fall of 1999, considered the design of work surfaces for use in microgravity environments, and another, considered Mars surface habitation strategies in the Fall semester of 2000. These projects were undertaken in collaboration with David Fitts of NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston.

Title: 2001 : Building for space travel - The history of space exploration in an art museum context
Publication: IAC 2001 congress proceedings, 52nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  1–5 October 2001, Toulouse, France
Abstract:
“Ars sine scientia nihil est,” or “Art without science is nothing.” So said the medieval French Master Mason Jean Mignot, referring to the ‘science’ of geometry that acted as the foundation for good proportions in architecture. Although attitudes in recent centuries have tended to compartmentalize the arts and sciences, two experiences at The Art Institute of Chicago have shown that the fine arts and science and technology all still co-exist within aerospace subjects. The first instance of this investigation was the 1996 exhibition, book, and series of public programs entitled Building for Air Travel. Architecture and Design for Commercial Aviation. This examined the role that architects, industrial designers, and graphic designers have played in creating airports, aircraft factories, airliner interiors and airline corporate identity over the past eight decades.
Our current exhibition and public interpretive project 2001: Building for Space Travel is a sequel to that very successful traveling exhibition on commercial aviation. 2001: Building for Space Travel examines the roles that architects and designers have played in the shaping of structures, interior spaces and corporate identity for space exploration, in reality as well as science fiction. The epic film 2001. A Space Odyssey is used as a focal point in the overall interpretation since even leading aerospace figures such as Wernher von Braun encouraged his designers and engineers to use that film as a source of inspiration to make space travel an everyday occurrence for all. Our project examines the role that design arts professionals have played in the history of space travel within three categories that are extensions of life and design activity on earth: our image .of the cosmos, before and after space travel; conflict in space; and exploration of the wilderness.
This paper will summarize the themes, installation, and public programs of 2001:Building for Space Travel at The Art Institute of Chicago in comparison with other activities within that museum’s Department of Architecture related to the history of aerospace technology, from exhibitions to archival collections. In so doing, it will present unique circumstances where a fine arts museum has endorsed and successfully implemented a series of programs related to aerospace design and technology.

Title: A STUDY OF GLOBAL MULTIMEDIA MOBILE SATELLITE COMMUNICATION SYSTEM
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
In Japan, the Ministry of Posts and
Telecommunications (MPT) conducted a feasibility
study in 1996 on a Next-generation LEO System
(NeLS) which would provide a global multimedia
mobile satellite service by means of a group of LEO
satellites with the user data rate up to 2 Mbps for handy
terminals. The target year for commercial
implementation is 2010. This concept is considered
the second phase of satellite component of the future
public land mobile telecommunications system (SFPLMTS)[
1] and the second generation of the big-LEO
systems. In order to develop the feasibility study, the
NeLS Research Center was formed by the
Telecommunications Advancement Organization of
Japan (TAO), in cooperation with the
telecommunications operators, manufacturers,
universities and governmental research organization in
the end of 1997.
According to the link budget calculations, the satellite
antenna diameter will be about 10 m in the S-band
system and about 5 m in the C-band system if the user
data rate of 2 Mbps is to be provided in the LEO
system. Assuming that the direct-radiating, active
phased array antenna technology is applied, the
satellite antenna (whose diameter is 5 to 10 m in the C-
/S- band) will need several thousand radiating elements,
each element being connected with a very small-sized
module consisting of filters, amplifiers, and digital
phase shifters.
Development of such a large-scale direct-radiating,
active phased array antenna would be one of the most
important breakthroughs. As a means of relaxing the
requirement of the satellite antenna design, the
realization of higher antenna gain in the user terminal
using the phased array technology should be also
investigated.
The inter-satellite link technology is also important,
because the inter-satellite network is essential to realize the low delay network connection for multimedia
services. ATM technology can be applicable for the
satellite on-board switch. However, new ATM control
algorithm should be developed for the LEO system.
This paper describes the service image, link budget
calculations, and key technologies to be developed in
the NeLS Research Center. As for the link budget,
two versions of calculations, original and revised ones,
are shown in the paper.

Title: Global Satellite Communications System for Asymmetric Multimedia Services
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
NTT has developed an asymmetrical
multimedia computer network that combines satellite
and terrestrial circuits111. This system provides
interactive communications between customer PCs and
servers. The forward signals (from servers to
customers) are transmitted by satellite circuits at a
transmission rate of approximately 30 M bit/s (in each
transponder), and the return signals (from customers to
servers) are transmitted by nanrow-band terrestrial
circuits. We provided the system for the Asian
Multimedia fomm (AMF)P1, and started to offer trial
services in Asia from this year. This paper presents a
newly developed piece of equipment called the ATM
satellite adapter, and describes the design objectives of
the bi-directional satellite links for the asymmetrical
multimedia computer network.
We have studied the next-generation global
system, which has sufficient functions for international
use. We suppose that satellite communication
circuits will have two important roles in the
multimedia era. One role is as the backbone network
between an information service provider and a hub node,
and the other is as a high-speed access network like the
DTH system. The construction of the high-speed
access network that use satellite circuits involves
determining a way of providing multimedia service to
areas that have no network infrastructure. We have
been stucfying a system that has satellite return links
(from customers to servers), in particular, the design
objectives of the return link. The system should have
a receiver that is small enough to be set up at a
customer’s building. We investigated a suitable
multiplex method and bit rate for the system.

Title: New Space: The Design and Form of the Extraterrestrial Garden
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
The garden has a special significance for human beings. In its diverse terrestrial shapes, the garden forms an important setting for many human activities. It seems likely that the attraction of the garden will not fade for humanity as it moves away from the Earth and into space. However, the particular design and form of the extraterrestrial garden is bound to be significantly different from its terrestrial equivalent, particularly in the terms of the human experience of time and change.
The garden may be conceptualised as ‘idea, place and action’. As ‘idea’ the garden signifies the illustration of an underlying function, philosophy, and aesthetic expressed through its design. As ‘place’ the garden exists as a physical space within which materials and objects may be arranged, all seen within the context of the surrounding environment. As ‘action’, the garden is a cause of human involvement both through its construction and preservation and through the experience of it.
This paper discusses existing terrestrial notions and forms of the garden, the importance of human perceptions and cultural viewpoints in gardens, the importance of the temporal element, and the concept of ‘idea, place and action’. These are then examined against the extraterrestrial context and factors influencing the design of the extraterrestrial gardens are described. Based on these, the ways in which the extraterrestrial garden might develop are discussed and some preliminary ideas for such presented.

Title: SECOND GENERATION GEOMOBILE SATELLITES - PROVIDING MOBILE AND RURAL MULTIMEDIA SERVICES
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
Satellites have been proven to be a solution
to national communications needs for an
instant deployment of service over a large
geographical area, offering every user a
flexible service of high quality. This paper
describes a design for a satellite based
turnkey communications system, providing
basic voice as well as advanced multimedia
services to rural areas. The system is
compatible with both handheld and small
fixed or transportable terminals. The overall
system architecture is described, stressing
an original turnkey approach and the key
features of space and ground segment. An
implementation strategy based on a recent
design for the EAST Company are
presented as well as compatibility issues for
an integrated satellite-terrestrial system
offering UMTS services.

Title: Use Of Lessons Learned to Enhance Payload Integration and Operations
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract: Payload operations involves the integration and flight of hardware that includes safety and mission success as the two highest priority elements. NASA intends to fully privatize Shuttle operations including marketing and flight of payloads in the near term and this transition is in its early stages. We have selected lessons learned from some of the more recent Shuttle payload flights in order to focus on areas where the contractor we could make an impact on future mission success. These include the preflight documents needed, payload testing, hazardous materials information, data required by the payload customer, hardware design, in-flight experience, and basic control center support. The payload project engineer is the focal point for the successful integration of customer requirements, and it is in this area that intervention can create the added value that makes a difference in the business aspect of payload operations. For integration and flight of cargo to/from the International Space Station (ISS), close attention must be paid to some of the more significant lessons learned as the move toward privatization continues.

Authors: ['C. Dionisio', 'S. Di Girolamo', 'F. Mura', 'A. Atzei', 'A. Martinez']
Title: Future Satellite Systems and Technologìes for Multimedia Services
Publication: IAC 1997 congress proceedings, 48th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–10 October 1997, Turin, Italy
Abstract:
Recently, Alenia Aerospazio has studied, under ESA contract (e.g. “Future Satellite Concepts, Architectures, Technologies and Service Capabilities” [1]), new architectures for communications satellite systems, in a long term fixture (i.e. 2010-2020). This paper deals only with a part of the total study, and it is not a summary of it. In fact this paper is relevant to the activity related to the communications systems; while the remote sensing applications, which have been studied too, will not be presented in this memory.
Starting from both service requirements and market analysis, the design of a future multimedia satellite system, based on six geostationary satellites, has been carried on, giving budget and performance for both payload and platform of each spacecraft.
As a result, several millions of mobile users (i.e. 6 millions of Palm Top at 128 Kbps, and 3 millions of Lap Top at 512 Kbps) and fixed users (i.e. 3000 of fixed stations at 1.2 Gbps) will be able to be served by this system.
The technology to be used for a fixture satellite payloads and platforms is the driving criteria to design a fixture multimedia system. Several candidate fixture technologies will be described in the paper: high temperature superconductors, fiber optic switches, multi chip modules for digital devices (3D-MCM), MEMS and smart materials, ultra light antennas and electro beam curing. For each technology, the priority and the improvement rationale will be given.
The driving business advantages have been outlined. The economic investigations, performed during the mentioned ESA study ([1]) will not be treated in this paper.

Title: OPTIMIZATION OF AN INFLATABLE MODULE FOR LUNAR/MARTIAN SURFACE
Publication: IAC 1997 congress proceedings, 48th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–10 October 1997, Turin, Italy
Abstract: A generic inflatable structure composed of identical modules for the Moon and/or Mars has been proposed. In order for this concept to be an optimal solution for a Lunar/Martian structure, a number of structural and functional criteria must be met. Structural optimization criteria include: carrying all loads without exceeding specified material strength limits; minimizing membrane thickness and therefore mass of the structure; and elimination or minimization of membrane wrinkling since this indicates inefficient use of the material; etc. Functional requirements include: stowability; easy deployment; outfitting; integration with airlocks; and others. A computer simulation consisting of a finite element analysis integrated with a 3D graphic model was applied to conduct a structural optimization of the module. This analysis demonstrated the feasibility of the inflatable module concept and improved upon the initial design. To date, the design and analysis has been based around an assumed set of material properties. Prior to finalization of the structural design, including material selection, the interaction of the structural and functional optimization criteria in the design process must be fully explored. An illustration and discussion of this process flow is presented.

Title: GLOBAL DESIGN OF SATELLITE CONSTELLATIONS : A MULTI-CRITERIA PERFORMANCE COMPARISON OF CLASSICAL WALKER PATTERNS AND NEW DESIGN PATTERNS
Publication: IAC 1996 congress proceedings, 47th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–11 October 1996, Beijing, China
Abstract:
Basically, the problem of designing a
multisatellite constellation exhibits a lot of
parameters with many possible
combinations : total number of satellites,
orbital parameters of each individual satellite,
number of orbital planes, number of satellites
in each plane, spacings between satellites of
each plane, spacings between orbital planes,
relative phasings between consecutive orbital
planes.
Hopefully, some authors have theoretically
solved this complex problem under
simplified assumptions : the permanent (or
continuous) coverage by a single and
multiple satellites of the whole earth and
zonal areas has been entirely solved from a
pure geometrical point of view. These
solutions exhibit strong symmetry properties
(e.g. : Walker, Ballard, Rider, Draim
constellations) : altitude and inclination are
identical, orbital planes and satellites are
regularly spaced, etc...
The problem with such constellations is their
oversimplified and restricted geometrical
assumption. In fact, the evaluation function
which is used implicitely only takes into
account the point-to-point visibility between
users and satellites and does not deal with
very important constraints and considerations
that become mandatory when designing a
real satellite system (e.g. : robustness to
satellite failures, total system cost, common
view between satellites and ground stations,
service availability and satellite reliability,
Launch and Early Operations Phase,
production constraints, etc...).
An original and global methodology relying
on a powerful optimisation tool based on
Genetic Algorithms has been developed at
ALCATEL ESPACE. In this approach,
symmetrical constellations can be used as
initial conditions of the optimization process
together with specific evaluation functions. A
multi-criteria performance analysis is
conducted and presented here in a parametric
way in order to identify and evaluate the
main sensitive parameters. Quantitative
results are given for three examples in the
fields of navigation, telecommunication and
multimedia satellite systems. In particular, a
new design pattern with very efficient
properties in terms of robustness to satellite
failures is presented and compared to
classical Walker patterns.

Title: Improvement of Russian Unmanned Space Capsules and their Infrastructure for Commercial Missions
Publication: IAC 1996 congress proceedings, 47th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–11 October 1996, Beijing, China
Abstract:
The Russian unmanned capsules, especially from the Foton family, offer an unique possibility for research under microgravity conditions. They are currently used for scientific payloads mainly in the field of materials research. The furnace facilities on board the capsules have already been widely used by European scientists for various material processing experiments. There is also an increasing commercial interest in processing materials in these facilities. Currently several ways are studied how to improve the Foton capsules, the furnace facilities the infrastructure (telemetry, telecommand, data storage, etc.) to attract more scientists and commercial customers.
VARIUS (Verbesserung der Attraktivitât russischer unbemannter Kapseln und deren Infrastruktur fur wissenschaftliche Expérimente und zum kommerziellen Einsatz) is a study analyzing the possibilities to commercialize the Russian Foton capsules and their infrastructure. This commercialization is built on a completely new finance model trading Russian foreign debts against space hardware. An agreement between the German and the Russian government on the barter transaction is currently in negotiation. Several feasibility studies are performed to start the barter as soon as possible.
The commercialization aspects that are studied in the frame of VARIUS comprise the identification of new markets and customers, the analysis of their requirements, the development of a business plan and the elaboration of new marketing strategies.
The Russian partners for this commercialization are the Central Specialized Design Bureau CSDB of Samara for the Foton capsules and the Technical Center SPLAY in Moscow for the furnace facilities. Both partners are involved in the study. They are working on technical improvements for the furnaces and the capsule infrastructure.
This paper will present the preliminary results of the feasibility study VARIUS, that is financially supported by the German Ministry for Economics and DARA.

Title: NEW ENTRY IN THE COMMERCIAL LAUNCH VEHICLE MARKET
Publication: IAC 1996 congress proceedings, 47th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–11 October 1996, Beijing, China
Abstract:
Rockwell International is now actively involved in the marketing and sale of the Cyclone launch vehicle. This paper summarizes the capabilities of this vehicle, describes launch operations and defines the Cyclone role within the spectrum of potential commercial launch opportunities.
A brief history of the Cyclone launch vehicle is presented, portraying its evolution and launch record. The Cyclone performance and operational characteristics are summarized, with special attention given to the integration approach, operational cycle, and time requirements for payload integration through completion of launch. Of particular interest is the relatively short time span needed to integrate and launch Cyclone payloads, with on-pad launch time typically less than 24 hours and sequential launches possible in less than 1 1/2 days.
An overview of the commercial satellite market is provided tracing historical trends andfuture market projections. These diverse and expanding commercial satellite systems are financially dependent upon successful orbital insertion of large numbers of satellites in a relatively short timeframe. This paper illustrates how the Cyclone launch vehicle is a viable solution to the commercial success of
these systems.______________________________

The Cyclone launch vehicle is one of the world’s most reliable space launchers with an impressive 97.9% success rate. This vehicle has been in operation for the past 30 years with over 200 launches to date. More than 20 Cyclone missions have involved multi- manifested payloads, all of them successfully launched. Both the two-stage Cyclone-2 and the three-stage Cyclone-3 are available for commercial launches to LEO at very cost effective prices. The expected lead time from contract to launch is only 18-24 months.
Two operational launch sites are currently available for commercial Cyclone launches:
• Plesetsk Spaceport in northern Russia
- primarily Cyclone-3 launches
• Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan
- primarily Cyclone-2 launches
With the Cyclone, a high performance LEO satellite launch vehicle for a variety of missions with a multi-manifested satellite approach is now available to the commercial satellite market. Yuzhnoye has considerable experience in the design and development of multiple satellite launch dispensers and other vehicle modifications. Its design team is now completing the launch dispenser system for the Globalstar system where 12 satellites will be deployed from each Zenit-2 launch vehicle. Like the Cyclone, the Zenit is also designed and produced in Ukraine by Yuzhnoye and Yuzhmash.
The team of Rockwell International’s Satellite Delivery Systems, the Yuzhnoye Design Office and the Yuzhmash Production Association are committed to the future expansion of the Cyclone launch vehicle into the worldwide commercial satellite market. Our joint experience base in launch vehicle design, production, payload integration and launch operations is the key element in this future marketing partnership.

Title: Stamps of the Space Race-Politics and Propaganda
Publication: IAC 1996 congress proceedings, 47th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–11 October 1996, Beijing, China
Abstract:
Due to their ubiquitous national circulation and international usage, stamps provide an effective vehicle for government propaganda, whether it be aimed at a domestic or international audience. Stamp illustration has proved to be a fertile field for the depiction of a tremendous range of subjects, with almost no topic is too obscure to appear on stamps. The birth of the Space Age gave rise to what is now one of the three most popular stamp collecting themes, astrophilately, but right from the outset space stamps became a propaganda weapon in the Cold War political contest between the United States and the USSR, as both sides vied to establish their ideological superiority through the technological successes of their space programs.
This paper will consider the use of space-themed stamps and associated philatelic materials, such as covers (envelopes), as propaganda tools during the Space Race. It will examine aspects of the iconography and design of many astrophilatelic items which indicate both overt and subtle propaganda intent, and attempt to relate them to contemporary political ideologies and national or international affairs.

Authors: ['E. Barbashov', 'V. Gavriliouk', 'V. Guriev', 'V. Isaev', 'A. Losenkov', 'E.V. Odintsov', 'A. Sobachkin', 'A. Sergienko']
Title: MATHEMATICAL MODELING OF PROPULSION SYSTEMS.
Publication: IAC 1995 congress proceedings, 46th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  2–6 October 1995, Oslo, Norway
Abstract: A set of mathematical models (already carefully validated), organized by module principle, is used for modeling working processes in different units of the rocket engine and engine on the whole. An important base feature is the possibility of flexible adaptation of the correspondent numerical methods and software for new design schemes of propulsion systems and its single units. Thus, this approach permits to save financial and time resources during design and test bend stage for prospective rocket engines. Special software is used for modeling starting, stopping regime, transition from one operating mode to another, emergency situations in engine. Original mathematical algorithm allows automatic generation of new code in case of piping system change, thus presented approach is sufficiently flexible for modifications during development of new engines. The results of this analysis are transferred for more detailed simulation of physical phenomena with use of 2D and 3D computations related to different engine units (combustion chambers, nozzles, gas generators, turbines, pump units). Illustrations of presented approach are given on the examples of typical hydrogen-oxygen large scale rocket engines.

Title: ON THE MERCURY MULTIPLE FLYBY MISSION VIA AN ELECTRIC PROPULSION
Publication: IAC 1995 congress proceedings, 46th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  2–6 October 1995, Oslo, Norway
Abstract: Multiple Mercury swingby technique has been applied to the Mercury exploration concept to provide sufficient payload mass. This paper investigates the use of an Solar Electric Propulsion (SEP) in the Mercury- Mercury transfer phase, taking the advantage of the solar power availability during the interplanetary cruising inside Earth orbit. The use of SEP upgrades the resultant spacecraft mass due to its high specific impulse. As an illustration, a small spacecraft design example is also presented.

Title: PHASE STABILIZATION OF FLEXIBLE MODES IN H DESIGN OF HIGHLY STABLE SATTELLITE ATTITUDE CONTROL SYSTEM
Publication: IAC 1995 congress proceedings, 46th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  2–6 October 1995, Oslo, Norway
Abstract: The ceaseless quest for enhanced pointing and stability for space missions demands improved attitude control system performance. The incresing size and complexity of spacecraft, with tighter pointing requirements poses a growing challenge for designing high performance attitude control systems. These spacecraft are flexible with flexure modes very near required control system bandwidth. Classical methods use either gain stabilization by notch filters or phase stabilization by appropriate compensators, and work well if the plant model taken is accurate. However, it is well known that in the course of modelling the spacecraft flexure modes, uncertainties or model inaccuracies creep in. Traditional design approaches limit the bandwidth to well below the lowest frequency flexible dynamics. The optimization method stands out as a comprehensive technique which handles stability, sensitivity and response shaping simultaneously. This paper highlights a method of phase stabilization of flexure modes (in the controller crossover region) of a spacecraft with flexible appendages using 11 X: designs. The proposed method provides for the required performance and robustness against model frequency and modal damping variations which are inevitable in spacecraft modeling. The control of the flexure modes is done with actuators and attitude sensors mounted on the central rigid body only. It is shown that the phase stabilization of the flexure modes (with a reasonable amount of uncertainty in the controller crossover region) is possible, in addition to achieving the desired performance objectives on pointing accuracy and platform stability. For illustration, simulation results showing the achieved performance with the method are presented.

Title: MULTILINGUAL MULTIMEDIA AEROSPACE GLOSSARY
Publication: IAC 1993 congress proceedings, 44th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–22 October 1993, Graz, Austria
Abstract:
A pilot multilingual multimedia aerospace glossary has been produced as part of Computer Aided Learning in Aerospace, a European Commission COMETT programme supported project, using a civil airliner as a subject example. It was initially developed on an Apple Macintosh platform, using the Authorware authoring system, and is being made available on IBM486PC, using Icon Author. The system provides visual image, verbal and text cues to the student in five languages (English,
French, German, Italian and Spanish), who can select routes through the aircraft from general configuration to design detailing. It uses Simplified Technical English, adopted by manufacturers and airlines, as a reference language. The system is easily adapted to related technical topics, and will be extended, with a satellite as subject to demonstrate its applicability to space engineering. If suitable hardware is available at the conference, the system will be demonstrated.

Title: SPACE TECHNOLOGY IN FILMS AND TELEVISION - PORTRAYAL AND PERCEPTION
Publication: IAC 1993 congress proceedings, 44th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–22 October 1993, Graz, Austria
Abstract:
One of the main ways in which the general public is introduced to space technology is through the fictional images of cinema films and television series. These media are primarily designed to entertain, rather than educate, but they often represent the only avenue by which the public learns of the wonders of space and the marvels of space technology.
This paper analyses the portrayal of space technology in a sample of films and TV series from pre-Sputnik days to the present. By considering the presentation of specific aspects of space technology, from overal1 spacecraft design to key subsystem technologies, conclusions are drawn as to their accuracy and the impression they are likely to make on the general public.
Recognising the constraints of film-making and marketing, the paper concludes by considering the extent to which film-makers contribute constructively to the cultural foundation of space activity.

Title: Commercialization strategies for space power technology
Publication: IAC 1990 congress proceedings, 41st  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–12 October 1990, Dresden, Germany
Abstract:
The Center for Space Power at Texas A&M University is one of sixteen Centers for the Commercial Development of Space established by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) to increase private-sector interest and investment in commercial space-related activities while stimulating advances in promising areas of research and development. The Center for Space Power uses the one million dollars received annually from NASA to cost-share space power research with industry sponsors. The research is usually performed by a university researcher, either individually or in collaboration with industry. In return for the sponsor’s involvement, the sponsor receives negotiated rights to any patents that might be derived from the research, the no-cost conduct of a research-related flight experiment onboard the Space Shuttle, and access to fairly inexpensive scientific and engineering talent from the associated university.
This paper presents a strategy for the commercialization of space power technology developed under the Center's sponsorship. The following example is illustrative of the commercialization being implemented by the Center for Space Power.
The concept of an orbiting power station providing electric power to docked or tethered spacecraft has been around since the early 1960s. The methods by which power can be delivered from an orbiting space station to one or more spacecraft include tethers that conduct energy between spacecraft at distances less than 1 km, transmission of energy at microwave or submillimeter wavelengths for distances less than 1000 km, and laser transmission. The utilization of tethers are severely limited by distance and mission considerations. And, laser transmission and energy conversion technologies are decades away from being mature enough to be practical.
In 1968, Dr. Peter Glaser proposed that spacecraft be linked by microwave power transmission to a central power station. This would increase the versatility of an orbiting power station. The technological expertise and experience to design and build an orbiting power generation station are available today. Only the transmission link between the power station and user spacecraft needs to be developed before a space power utility can become a commercial reality. Recent advancements in microwave technologies indicate that the development of a commercial intra-space microwave transmission system is both practical and achievable within this decade.
With the development of special-purpose microwave transmitters and rectifier antennae (or rectennae), a working prototype of a microwave power transmission system is near at hand. The flight experiments sponsored by the Center for Space Power and industrial affiliates will demonstrate a prototype system within the next few years. By the turn of the century, the technology to construct an orbiting power station utilizing a microwave power transmission system will be available.
The formation of a multi-national, industrial consortium is being promoted by the Center for Space Power in association with Arthur D. Little, Inc., to fund the development and marketing of an orbiting power station. The orbiting power station will be owned and operated as an independent space power utility company supplying the needs of one or more space platforms and spacecraft. This would relieve the space industry in general of the need to be in the power business, and permit the concentration of power system expertise to reside with the space power utility for greater efficiency and economy. With the appropriate support and commitment, a space power utility system (i.e., an orbiting power generation station and microwave power transmission system) can be operational by the year 20 10.

Title: Infrared extra solar planet detection with the Hubble space telescope
Publication: IAC 1989 congress proceedings, 40th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–13 October 1989, Malaga, Spain
Abstract: NICMOS, a second generation near infrared instrument for the HST, offers a new opportunity for the detection of planets and other substellar objects around nearby stars. Coronagraphic techniques exploit the lower scattered light at infrared wavelengths to aid in detection. The reduction in scattered light is offset by the larger area of the Airy ring to produce a planetary signal-to-noise ratio similar to the optical region. Unique opportunities afforded by the absorption spectrum of giant gaseous planets and the infrared luminosity of brown dwarfs are available at near infrared wavelengths. Several aspects of NICMOS such as pixel size, corona- graphic design and ultimate sensitivity are designed to utilize these advantages.

Title: Hermes thermal protection system overview
Publication: IAC 1986 congress proceedings, 37th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  4–11 October 1986, Innsbruck, Austria
Abstract:
As a first step of its Spacelab follow-on programme towards space station design and utilization, the European Space Agency (ESA) initiated end 1984 the development of a European Retrievable Carrier, called EURECA. This carrier project will provide the Agency with valuable early experience in the development, utilization, and operation of unmanned, automated platforms in low earth orbits.
Scheduled for launch in March 1988, EURECA will be delivered by the Space Shuttle into an orbital altitude of 296 km, will ascend to an operational altitude of about 500 km, and will return to the lower orbit after 6 to 9 months to be retrieved by the Shuttle. The major objectives of the first EURECA mission are to perform material science experiments. However, in order to demonstrate its flexibility, the first payload also includes experiments in the field of solar and astrophysics, as well as technical demonstrations of a European Radio Ionization Thruster Assembly (RITA) and direct inter-orbit Communications (IOC) via the Olympus Communications Satellite with the central European Operations Center (ESOC) in Darmstadt, Germany.
In describing the concept of EURECA, this paper highlights the most important design considerations for the sizing, development, operations, and utilization of EURECA. As an illustration of its adaptability to mission needs of various disciplines, a summary of the latest payload accommodation studies, and advanced mission planning data, are included.

Title: The munic hailstorm of July 12, 1984 - A lesson, how urgent we need improved satellite and radar monitoring for a better disaster warning
Publication: IAC 1986 congress proceedings, 37th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  4–11 October 1986, Innsbruck, Austria
Abstract:
The National Aeronautics and Space Administration Space Station Program now underway will be the centerpiece around which a major segment of the U.S. civil space program of the future will be structured. It will be an orbiting laboratory, test center, manufacturing site, and observation platform that will open broad new areas of opportunities for the users of space.
The Space Station Program planning activity started with a focus on potential mission requirements, architecture and technology. All types of potential users have been active, including representatives of the science and applications communities, industry,and commercial interests, and technology development organizations. In addition, there is commercial interest in secondary spinoffs of technology and marketing of products that would use material or methods developed or produced in space. Given this preliminary work, the definition studies of design and configuration have started with a solid appreciation of what users must be able to do.

Title: Life prediction of CIP formed thrust chamber
Publication: IAC 1985 congress proceedings, 36th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–12 October 1985, Stockholm, Sweden
Abstract:
This paper provides an overview of a study by Lockheed's Biotechnology organization conducted for NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center. The objectives of the study were to establish the most efficient systems analysis and design tools and methods for the accommodation of life sciences research facilities on space stations and platforms.
The detailed contract reports create the engineering and programmatic data base for NASA to procédé with space station life sciences facilities planning. Samples of that work in this paper show the wealth of design data that has been catalogued and curves of parametric relationships that have been derived for use in the design trade studies already conducted and anticipated in the future. Roadmaps which will guide concept development and support programmatic sensitivity studies are illustrated.
A computer program called Microcomputer Mission Integration and Accommodation Algorith (MMISIAA) was developed to permit desktop manipulation of plant and animal vivarium and laboratory instrumentation design data. Illustrations of its outputs are shown.
The paper is organized in accordance with the contract tasks as follows: parameter analysis, tradeoff analyses, and conceptual design requirements. Sample concepts are discussed for three different mission assumptions.

Title: The SPOT-HRV instrument: An overview of design and performance
Publication: IAC 1983 congress proceedings, 34th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–15 October 1983, Budapest, Hungary
Abstract:
The HRV (High Visible Resolution) is an Earth Resource Sensor built by MATRA for CNES for the SPOT series of spacecraft. The SPOT spacecraft will be placed into orbit early in 1985.
After a brief review of the basic SPOT mission features, this paper deals with :
1. Detailed description of HRV performance requirements, system and main sub-system design, and technologies involved.
2. Typical problem areas involving extensive design trade-off analysis and testing. Two detailed examples are used as illustrations:
- mechanical design and thermal distortion analysis and results
- signal-to-noise analysis and calibration considerations.
Keywords - High Resolution Visible, SPOT,
Earth Remote Sensor, Charge coupled Device,
Off-Nadir Viewing, on-board computer

Title: Parameter invariable compensation control system of a spaceship into space of an atmospheric descent
Publication: IAC 1976 congress proceedings, 27th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–16 October 1976, Anaheim, United States
Abstract:
The Technique is considered to select the equivalent of adaptive control system structure and parameters for the plant with varying parameters. This system utilizes the physically realizable linear corrective loops. The measurable plant coordinates are angular rate and normal G—load.
As illustration of the technique the reusable vehicle descent control system design is given. It is shown that during the descent almost all dynamical properties of the stabilization system can remain in determined limits.

Title: Piloted simulators for space research
Publication: IAC 1965 congress proceedings, 16th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  13–18 October 1965, Athens, Greece
Abstract:
Man is an essential element in many of our space programs. In exploring the unknown only man can observe the unpredictable or react intelligently to the unexpected. Not only do we need man in space as an explorer and observer but we also need his capabilities in the management and control of our missions in order to improve their reliability and chances of success. To take full advantage of man’s unique attributes we must study his capabilities, define them, and then using this information design our space systems so that he becomes an integral part of the mission. These objectives are accomplished through the use of manned flight simulators.
This paper discusses a variety of manned flight simulations that are particularly applicable to space research. Most of the simulators described are in operation, but rae relatively new. Some of the simulators are still under construction or in the planning stage. A few of the simulators are nonexistent—that is, although the research problems have been defined no satisfactory methods for adequately simulating the problems have been found. The facilities described have been selected either because they present new and novel methods for simulating some of the peculiar aspects of the space environment or because they contain unique construction or operational features that may have application to other simulation facilities.

Title: Synchronous communications satellites
Publication: IAC 1965 congress proceedings, 16th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  13–18 October 1965, Athens, Greece
Abstract:
A synchronous satellite is one which orbits at an altitude of 36,000 km, where its orbital period matches that of the Earth’s rotation. If the orbit is also circular and equatorial, the satellite appears stationary when viewed from the Earth. The advantages of the synchronous orbit for communications satellites have long been recognized, but only within recent years has a practical design evolved for such a satellite. Syncom 2, launched 26 July 1963, was the world’s first synchronous satellite; Syncom 3, launched 19 August 1964, was the first stationary satellite; Early Bird, launched 6 April 1965, is the first commercial communications satellite, and it also is in a geo-stationary orbit. The accumulated operational life to date of these satellites is nearly four years, and all are still functioning properly.
These satellites, despite their impressive record in both military and civil communications, represent just the initial generation in the evolution of synchronous satellites. Advanced models in design and under test will have much higher power and bandwidth and improved stationkeeping capability, and will make possible radically new types of communication service within the next few years. But all are based on the same fundamental design features which made synchronous satellites practical much sooner than had been anticipated. These features are illustrated in the accompanying illustrations.
Configuration photographs of Syncom are shown in Figs. 1 and 2. In Fig. 2 the solar panels have been removed to show the locations and sizes of the equipment complement. The communication repeaters, telemetry and command systems, control systems, and apogee kick rocket are visible.

Title: Same title as paper # 1963-37
Publication: IAC 1963 congress proceedings, 14th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  25 September–1 October 1963, Paris, France
Abstract:
The technology of satellite launchings and space vehicles has gone a long way since the first sputnik launchings in 1957. The first interest has mainly been directed towards the power and performance of a space vehicle as one would expect. Most of the possible applications of space flight, however, will not merely ask for a certain payload to be injected into a cosmic trajectory but the accuracy with which this can be done is of equal importance and might even be the primary requirement. Accuracy without payload would be nonsensical and therefore the payload evaluations for a given configuration, the form of guidance and the achieved final accuracy are intimately connected with each other. Strictly speaking, another technical aspect, namely the reliability has also to be brought into the picture.
This lecture, therefore, makes an attempt to look at the problems of guiding a space vehicle bearing in mind those general points. In considering the guidance of a space vehicle one must avoid making two fundamental mistakes. The first is the “classical” approach, still very often used in aircraft design. The structure and the power unit are designed and then the control and guidance problems are solved as an afterthought. This approachÿr doomed to failure especially when the payload envisaged is tending to be marginal. In such a case it is imperative that the study of guidance commences in parallel with the performance calculations and the general design study.
The other common error is the opposite, namely the “doing too much of a good thing” which gives sometimes the impression that a whole mission is only carried out ip order to prove a complex and sophisticated form of guidance.
It is very important not to forget that “guidance” is actually a nuisance, a necessary evil, which will consume valuable payload. It should, therefore, be the foremost task of the guidance engineer to find the simplest possible solution, in this way assuring that the vehicle borne weight is a minimum. This is in most cases equivalent to achieving the maximum reliability.
Although all guidance problems in space have common features and similar solutions it is advisable to keep to a specific example. For this lecture, the launching of the E.L.D.O. vehicle into a circular orbit of 550 km height above the Earth’s surface has been chosen. When appropriate, a more complex mission, the lauching of a synchronous communication satellite will bemsed as an illustration of the problems involved.
The main purpose of this lecture is not so much to giv'e an agreed solution ready Jor use. It is rather intended to list the problems. Furthermore it will be shown that the simplification expressed by the departure from the strict thcg^ctical solution can be carried very far before the errors incurred by such a process will be significant.

Title: The manhigh II balloon operation
Publication: IAC 1957 congress proceedings, 8th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–12 October 1957, Barcelona, Spain
Abstract:
The paper I presented at this Congress entitled “10 Years of Plastic Balloons” describes the new plastic balloon vehicle and some of its research applications. Currently, the modern balloon is the only vehicle with which it is possible to carry out extended manned flights under space-equivalent conditions with a current capability of reaching altitudes above 99 % of the earth’s atmosphere. It is an ideal laboratory and aerial observatory for many experiments.
I have been asked to speak in more detail of one of the applications discussed in my paper, namely the last Manhigh balloon flight. My other paper shows some illustrations of this project. I will speak about the part for which Winzen Research Inc. was responsible, the design and construction of the balloon and the gondola as well as the flight operation itself. Following this talk, Major Simons will discuss the Manhigh flight from the point of view of the pilot inside the gondola.2
